Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- After a nearly decade-long effort, the National Congress of Black Women on Tuesday honored Sojourner Truth by making her the first African-American woman to have a memorial bust in the U.S. Capitol. Speaker Nancy Pelosi and first lady Michelle Obama applaud the unveiling of the Sojourner Truth bust. Truth, whose given name was Isabella Baumfree, was a slave who became one of the most respected abolitionists and women's rights activists. "One could only imagine what Sojourner Truth, an outspoken, tell-it-like-it-is kind of woman ... what she would have to say about this incredible gathering," first lady Michelle Obama said at the Celebration of Truth ceremony. "We are all here because, as my husband says time and time again, we stand on the shoulders of giants like Sojourner Truth." "And just as Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott would be pleased to know that we have a woman serving as the speaker of the House of Representatives, I hope that Sojourner Truth would be proud to see me, a descendant of slaves, serving as the first lady of the United States of America," she said. Dignitaries and congressional leaders, including Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, House Republican Leader John Boehner and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, attended the ceremony marking the unveiling of the statue. Along with musical performances, actress Cicely Tyson recited "Ain't I A Woman," Truth's famous 1851 speech to a women's rights convention. Clinton and Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee, who worked together to draft legislation to commission the bust, were among speakers who paid tribute to the late C. Delores Tucker, former chairwoman of the NCBW, who spearheaded the effort for the Truth memorial. "What a wonderful day it is to be here in Emancipation Hall for this great occasion when Sojourner Truth takes her rightful place alongside the heroes who have helped to shape our nation's history," Clinton said. "Today, she takes her place in this Capitol, and we are the better for it," Clinton said. "She is a sojourner of truth, by truth, and for truth. And her words, her example and her legacy will never perish from this earth, so long as men and women stand up and say loudly and clearly, 'We hear you echoing down through the years of history. We believe that your journey is not yet over, and we will make the rest of that journey with you.' " The bronze statue, which was crafted by Los Angeles, California, sculptor Artis Lane, will stand in Emancipation Hall at the Capitol Visitor Center. "All the visitors in the U.S. Capitol will hear the story of brave women who endured the greatest of humanity's indignities. They'll hear the story of Sojourner Truth, who didn't allow those indignities to destroy her spirit, who fought for her own freedom and then used her powers ... to help others," Michelle Obama said. "The power of this bust will not just be in the metal that delineates Sojourner Truth's face; it will also be in the message that defines her legacy. Forevermore, in the halls of one of our country's greatest monuments of liberty and equality, justice and freedom, Sojourner Truth's story will be told again and again and again and again." In 1997, Congress passed a special act that called for relocating the Portrait Monument from the Capitol basement to the rotunda. The 7.5-ton statue depicts three leaders of the suffragette movement -- Anthony, Stanton and Mott. A group called the Sojourner Truth Crusade was upset about the statue's relocation because it didn't incorporate Truth. After Congress agreed to go ahead with a move, advocates proposed commissioning a new statue that would include Truth. In 2006, Congress passed a bill to honor the abolitionist with her own memorial.

(CNN) — Following almost 10 years of advocacy, the National Congress of Black Women paid tribute to Sojourner Truth on Tuesday with the unveiling of her memorial bust, making her the first Black woman represented by a bust in the U.S. Capitol.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and first lady Michelle Obama applauded as the sculpture was revealed. Truth, born Isabella Baumfree, escaped slavery and went on to become a prominent abolitionist and campaigner for women’s rights.

Speaking at the Celebration of Truth ceremony, Obama reflected on what Truth—known for her candid and forceful manner—might have thought about the extraordinary gathering. She said those in attendance owed much to towering historical figures such as Truth, echoing President Obama’s frequent observation that the present generation stands on the shoulders of giants.

Obama added that Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott likely would have welcomed seeing a woman become speaker of the House. In the same way, she said, she hoped Truth would take pride in seeing a descendant of enslaved people serve as the nation’s first lady.

The event brought together numerous officials and congressional leaders, including Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, House Republican Leader John Boehner and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

The ceremony also featured music, while actress Cicely Tyson delivered a recitation of “Ain’t I A Woman,” the celebrated speech Truth gave at a women’s rights convention in 1851.

Clinton and Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee, who jointly developed the legislation authorizing the bust, were among those who honored the late C. Delores Tucker. Tucker, a former chairwoman of the National Congress of Black Women, had led the campaign to establish a memorial to Truth.

Clinton described the unveiling in Emancipation Hall as a historic moment in which Truth was finally placed among the figures who helped form the nation’s history. She said Truth’s presence in the Capitol strengthened the institution and declared that the activist’s message, life and influence would endure as long as people continued to recognize her call and carry forward her unfinished work.

Created in bronze by Los Angeles sculptor Artis Lane, the bust will remain in Emancipation Hall inside the Capitol Visitor Center.

Michelle Obama said Capitol visitors would now learn about courageous women who survived some of humanity’s worst abuses. They would also hear how Truth refused to let those experiences break her, secured her own freedom and then devoted her abilities to helping other people.

According to Obama, the sculpture’s significance would come not only from the bronze used to portray Truth’s features, but also from the principles embodied in her legacy. She said Truth’s life would continue to be recounted throughout the Capitol, one of the country’s foremost symbols of freedom, equality, liberty and justice.

The path to the memorial began in 1997, when Congress approved special legislation directing that the Portrait Monument be moved from the Capitol basement to the rotunda. Weighing 7.5 tons, that monument portrays three leading figures in the women’s suffrage movement: Anthony, Stanton and Mott.

The Sojourner Truth Crusade objected to the relocation because the monument did not include Truth. Once Congress decided to proceed with the move, supporters called for a separate sculpture that would feature her. In 2006, lawmakers passed legislation authorizing an individual memorial to honor the abolitionist.

After a campaign that lasted nearly a decade, national leaders gathered at the U.S. Capitol on April 28, 2009, to unveil a memorial bust of Sojourner Truth, the formerly enslaved abolitionist and pioneering advocate for women’s rights. The effort was led by the National Congress of Black Women and advanced through legislation authorizing the memorial. Created by sculptor Artis Lane, the bronze bust was installed in Emancipation Hall in the Capitol Visitor Center.

The ceremony brought together members of Congress, activists, and other dignitaries, including First Lady Michelle Obama, House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton, and Representative Sheila Jackson Lee. Speakers emphasized both Truth’s extraordinary life and the significance of finally giving her a permanent place among the historical figures honored in the Capitol.

Born into slavery in New York around 1797 as Isabella Baumfree, Truth escaped with her infant daughter in 1826. She later successfully went to court to recover a son who had been illegally sold, becoming one of the first Black women in the United States to prevail in such a case against a white man. In 1843, she adopted the name Sojourner Truth and devoted herself to traveling and speaking against slavery and in favor of equal rights. Her forceful speeches—most famously associated with the 1851 women’s rights convention in Akron, Ohio—challenged a society that often excluded Black women from both abolitionist and women’s suffrage movements.

Truth continued her activism during and after the Civil War. She supported the Union cause, helped recruit Black soldiers, advocated assistance for formerly enslaved people, and pressed the federal government to protect their rights. She also campaigned for women’s suffrage and for broader economic and political opportunities for African Americans until her death in 1883.

The unveiling represented a historic milestone: Truth became the first African American woman to be honored with a memorial bust in the U.S. Capitol. The distinction also underscored how long Black women’s contributions had been overlooked in the nation’s most prominent public spaces. More than a tribute to one individual, the memorial acknowledged Truth’s central role in the struggles for emancipation, citizenship, and gender equality.

By placing her likeness in the Capitol, the nation formally recognized a woman whose courage and moral clarity helped reshape American democracy. The bust stands as a reminder of the barriers Truth confronted, the movements she helped advance, and the generations of women and Black leaders who drew inspiration from her example.

The sculpture is the first in the Capitol’s art collection to honor an African American woman.

The ceremony marked the culmination of a roughly decade-long effort led by the National Congress of Black Women, which raised private funds, rallied lawmakers and pressed for congressional authorization to place Truth’s likeness in the Capitol.

“I hope that Sojourner Truth would be proud to see me, a descendant of slaves, serving as first lady of the United States of America,” Obama told the audience.

Its placement, she said, was not simply about adding another work of art but about broadening the story the Capitol tells about American democracy.

Clinton, who supported the project while serving as first lady and later as a U.S. senator from New York, recalled meeting with leaders of the National Congress of Black Women and learning that no statue or bust of a Black woman was then displayed in the Capitol.

“What I remember most was the shock that so many of us felt,” Clinton said of that realization. The campaign that followed, she added, ensured that Truth’s courage would be visible to millions of visitors.

Pelosi praised Truth as a figure who challenged both racial oppression and the exclusion of women from political life. Truth “did not accept the world as it was,” Pelosi said, but instead worked to make it what it should be.

Among those recognized during the program were Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas, a principal congressional advocate for the bust; leaders of the National Congress of Black Women, including its president, E. Faye Williams; and the late civil-rights activist C. DeLores Tucker, the organization’s founding chair and an early driving force behind the project. Lane, a nationally known sculptor and painter, was also honored for creating the work.

Congress formally authorized acceptance of the privately funded bust through legislation signed into law in 2006. Jackson Lee championed the measure in the House, while Clinton helped advance the effort in the Senate. The law directed the Joint Committee on the Library to accept the sculpture on behalf of Congress and arrange for its display in a prominent Capitol location.

Lane based the bronze on surviving photographs of Truth, seeking to capture the abolitionist’s age, dignity and determination rather than present an idealized image. The finished work depicts Truth wearing a shawl and bonnet, her expression steady and direct.

Born into slavery as Isabella Baumfree in Ulster County, New York, around 1797, Truth was sold several times as a child and spoke Dutch before learning English. She escaped slavery with her infant daughter in 1826, a year before New York completed gradual emancipation.

She later went to court to recover a son who had been illegally sold into slavery in Alabama — and won, becoming one of the first Black women known to have successfully challenged a white man in an American court.

In 1843, she adopted the name Sojourner Truth and began traveling as a preacher and lecturer. She became a powerful voice for abolition, women’s rights and equal citizenship. Her best-known speech, delivered at a women’s-rights convention in Akron, Ohio, in 1851, became associated with the refrain “Ain’t I a Woman?” Although later versions differ from contemporary accounts of her remarks, the speech has endured as a defining challenge to racism and sexism.

During the Civil War, Truth recruited Black soldiers for the Union Army and gathered supplies for formerly enslaved people. She later worked with the Freedmen’s Bureau in Washington and met President Abraham Lincoln at the White House in 1864. After the war, she continued pressing for voting rights, land and economic independence for freed people until her death in Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1883.
